samples.summary: New "no opener at all" test asserts the mock's shape, not the behavior the comment claims
samples.evidence: `it('resolves when there is no opener at all')` (login-callback.test.ts:198-204) sets `openMock.mockRejectedValueOnce(new Error('no opener'))` and asserts `openBrowser(...)` resolves. Because `open` is fully module-mocked (line 21), the premise the new 20-line comment block (lines 168-181) is built on — that a missing opener binary surfaces as a *rejection* from `open()` rather than as a `nextTick` `error` event on a child, because open v11 attaches `once('error', reject)` synchronously with `spawn()` — is asserted nowhere; it is simply encoded in the mock. If open ever changed that ordering (or the `try` were narrowed), this test would still pass while the real CLI died mid-login. What the test does prove is only that `openBrowser` has a `try/catch` around an awaited rejection, which is a much weaker statement than the comment sells. Not a blocker: the un-mocked behavior is arguably untestable here, but the comment should not present mock-shaped coverage as verification of open's internals.

samples.summary: No test covers `open()` resolving without a child process (`child?.on?.` guard)
samples.evidence: `openBrowser` guards with double optional chaining: `child?.on?.('error', () => {})` (login.ts:122). The two tests in `describe('openBrowser')` cover only (a) a resolved value that IS an EventEmitter (line 187) and (b) a rejection (line 198). Nothing drives `openMock.mockResolvedValueOnce(undefined)` or a resolved value lacking `.on` — the case both `?.`s exist for (open resolves `undefined` on some platforms/wsl paths). Dropping either `?.` would not fail this suite even though it would throw inside a real login. Note the default module mock at line 21 (`vi.fn(async () => undefined)`) does return undefined, but no test in this describe block exercises `openBrowser` against it directly with an assertion about that path.
